uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a1.text: On a moonlit night, this squid has a problem: its own shadow.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a2.text: This is the Hawaiian bobtail squid. It's active at night. And seen from below, it would be a dark shape against the moon.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a3.text: So it glows from underneath, matching the moonlight above. And the shadow disappears.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a5.text: But the light isn't made by the squid. It's made by bacteria.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a5b.text: They live in a pouch on the squid's underside, called the light organ. It even has a reflector, and a lens, to aim their glow downwards.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a6.text: They're called Aliivibrio fischeri. Until 2007, they were Vibrio fischeri.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a7.text: And here's the strange part. These bacteria only glow when there are lots of them. Alone in the open sea, they stay dark.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a8.text: So how does a single cell know it's in a crowd?

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b1.text: Each cell leaks a little signal molecule into the water around it.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b2.text: When cells are few, the signal drifts away.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b3.text: When many cells are packed together, it builds up.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b4.text: And past a certain level, a threshold, the genes switch on across the whole crowd.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b6.text: A quorum is the smallest number of members who must be present before a meeting can make decisions.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b7.text: The word is Latin, for 'of whom'.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b8.text: The signal itself is called an autoinducer.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:b9.text: The first clue came in 1970, from glowing marine bacteria. Their light only switched on once the cells had built up something in their own broth: a substance they made themselves.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c1.text: So what's going on inside one of those cells?

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c2.text: An enzyme called LuxI makes the signal. It's called an AHL, short for acyl-homoserine lactone: a small ring, with a fatty tail.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c3.text: In the squid's bacteria, it's small enough to slip straight through the cell's membrane. In and out.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c4.text: Inside, a protein called LuxR waits.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c5.text: When enough signal has built up, LuxR grabs it, and switches on the light genes.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c6.text: And one of those genes is luxI itself.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c7.text: So the more signal there is, the more signal gets made.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c8.text: In the open sea, the signal never builds up. Packed into the squid's light organ, it does. And they glow.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c9.text: The bacteria pay their rent in light.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c10.text: Every dawn, the squid evicts most of them anyway. Ninety percent or more, vented into the sea.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d1.text: Not every bacterium speaks the same chemical language.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d2.text: The squid's bacteria use AHLs. So does Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d3.text: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus use something else: short chains of amino acids. Tiny protein fragments.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d4.text: The cell pumps them out, and they're mostly caught by receptors on the cell's surface.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d5.text: And one signal, called AI-2, is made by many different kinds of bacteria.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:d6.text: Some scientists think it may work as a shared word between species. That's still debated.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e1.text: So what do bacteria do, once they know they're a crowd?

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e2.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses its count to time an attack.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e3.text: While it's few, it holds back most of its weapons.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e4.text: Once there are enough, it switches on toxins, and enzymes that damage tissue. Virulence factors: the tools a microbe uses to cause disease.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e5.text: And it builds a biofilm: a slimy, protected city of cells.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e6.text: Scientists think waiting may keep it from being noticed too early. Attack with a few cells, and the immune system wins.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e7.text: Patience, it turns out, is a virulence factor.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e8.text: Vibrio cholerae, the bacterium behind cholera, does the opposite.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e9.text: When there are few of them, they stick to the gut wall, and make their toxin.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e10.text: When the crowd gets big, the same switch turns all that off. Scientists think it helps them let go, and leave.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:e11.text: And its way out of the body is the disease itself. The toxin it made earlier causes the diarrhoea that carries it out.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f1.text: If bacteria act on a signal, can the signal be jammed?

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f2.text: It can. Some bacteria make enzymes that break the AHL's ring open. This is called quorum quenching.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f3.text: One, from a Bacillus, was given to a bacterium that rots plants. The rot became much weaker.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f4.text: A red seaweed from Australian waters, Delisea pulchra, makes molecules shaped like the signal. They jam the receiver.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f5.text: And its surface stays remarkably clean of bacteria.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f6.text: Drugs that jam the signal, instead of killing the bacteria, are being studied. None is a standard treatment yet.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f7.text: One last thing. Bacteria don't actually count heads.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f8.text: They sense how concentrated the signal is.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f9.text: So a few cells in a tight space can reach the threshold. And a big crowd in open, flowing water may never reach it.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f10.text: In one experiment, a single Staphylococcus aureus cell, sealed in a tiny droplet, switched on its quorum-sensing genes all by itself.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f11.text: No crowd. Just a very small room.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:f12.text: The scientists think this may happen inside the body, too: when a bacterium is swallowed by an immune cell, and trapped in a tiny pocket.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:w1.text: That's quorum sensing. One small molecule, building up in the dark, until a crowd of cells knows it's time.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a6b.text: Then a study of their DNA showed they sit on a branch of their own, so they got a new name: Aliivibrio. The other Vibrio.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:a6c.text: Many researchers still use the old one.

uk7wwhXdWYHKKZ8KTCVw:c7b.text: And the cells make this inducer themselves. That's the 'auto' in autoinducer.
